reconstructed_article: The Freewinds, a ship owned by the Church of Scientology, was sealed in April 2008 in Curaçao, where public health officials began investigating the presence of blue asbestos. According to The Daily Herald and Lloyd's List, work on the ship's interior was suspended on April 27 after health inspectors found traces of blue asbestos. Samples taken from paneling were sent to the Netherlands, where analysis revealed significant levels of blue asbestos. An April 25 inspection involved Frank Esser, interim director of the Curaçao Drydock Company; Christiene van der Biezen, Curaçao's head of labor affairs; Tico Ras, head of the local health department; and two inspectors. Panama Maritime Authority director Alfonso Castillero stated an investigation was underway. Lawrence Woodcraft, a former Scientologist and licensed architect, supervised work on the ship in 1987 and attested to the presence of blue asbestos in a 2001 online statement. He reported his findings to Church of Scientology executives at the time. The Church of Scientology purchased the ship, then known as the Bohème, in 1987 through Flag Ship Trust, and put it into service in June 1988 for advanced Scientology training and spiritual retreats. Church spokeswoman Karin Pouw stated that air quality inspections in April confirmed the Freewinds meets U.S. standards. A team from the United States traveled to Curaçao to remove asbestos. A May 15 statement to a UK newspaper said there has never been asbestos exposure on the Freewinds.

reconstructed_article: The Victorian Government has approved a $380 million wind farm at Mount Gellibrand in the state's south-west. Planning Minister Rob Hulls announced the approval, describing the project as Australia's most powerful and Victoria's largest wind farm to date. The project is expected to create between 110 and 120 jobs during construction and up to 25 full-time positions during the wind farm's operational life. The wind farm will be located 120 km west of Melbourne, close to the regional centre of Colac. It will comprise 116 turbines of the 2 MW class, with an overall capacity of 232 MW. The facility is expected to produce over 700,000 MWh annually, enough to supply approximately 132,000 Victorian households. German company Pro Ventum International is undertaking the project. Minister Hulls said nine objections had been lodged against the project. Local landowner Tim Gore, who plans to have 32 turbines on his property, said he was not concerned about potential noise. Pro Ventum International said it would commence work on an Environmental Management report in the coming weeks. Wind farm critic Tim Le Roy said there was no environmental benefit from the project and the Victorian Government would better spend its money elsewhere. In October of the previous year, Colac Otway council chief executive officer Tracey Slatter said the proposal would benefit the shire by reducing greenhouse gas emissions and addressing increasing energy demand.

On Friday, 178 plaintiffs, including construction workers and family members of deceased workers, filed a lawsuit in Tokyo, Japan, seeking approximately 6.6 billion yen (about 64 million USD) in damages from the Japanese government and 46 building manufacturers. Reports indicate this is the first class action in Japan related to health damages from asbestos exposure at construction sites. The plaintiffs are from Tokyo and surrounding areas.

They claim the government and manufacturers knew of the dangers of asbestos inhalation but failed to take proper precautions, including not ceasing to promote asbestos as a cheap construction material and not banning its production. After inhaling asbestos in the workplace, 172 people developed lung cancer or mesothelioma, and nearly half of those afflicted have died.

Plaintiffs argue the government and health ministry did not act quickly enough after international organizations issued warnings in 1972 that asbestos could be a carcinogen. They also blame the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry for sanctioning asbestos use under the Factory Act, and the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure, Transport and Tourism for approving asbestos-containing materials under Japan's Building Standards Law.

Approximately 40 construction workers plan to file a similar lawsuit in June. Following a 2005 revelation that residents near a factory developed asbestos-related diseases, the government implemented a 2006 law providing monetary assistance to victims and relatives. Plaintiffs argue the assistance is insufficient. Japan banned the spraying of asbestos in 1975.

reconstructed_article: Around 500 melon-headed whales were sighted swimming near the shores of Pilar, Bataan, about 135 kilometers northwest of Manila, at approximately 4:00 a.m. on Tuesday. Philippine Coast Guard commander Luis Tuazon and Bataan Governor Enrique Garcia Jr. reported the sighting. More than 100 fishermen and volunteers, along with personnel from the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR), local police, and the Coast Guard, used dozens of fishing boats with engines off to guide the whales toward deeper waters by clapping and hitting the water surface. The mammals were initially misidentified as dolphins but were later identified as melon-headed whales by local veterinarian Mariel Flores. Four dead whales were found in Abucay and Tortugas, including two adult females—one pregnant and one that had given birth to a calf that also died. A necropsy by Dr. Lemnuel Aragones of the University of the Philippines found the two adults had damaged eardrums. Provincial veterinarian Alberto Venturina said the adults weighed 250 to 300 kilograms, and the calf was about one month old. BFAR director Malcolm Sarmiento Jr. said this was the largest stranding recorded, with previous events involving only 20 to 30 animals. By 4:30 p.m., the whales were guided back to deeper waters. Possible causes discussed included underwater earthquakes, chemical pollution, dynamite fishing, and a sea floor earthquake study conducted by the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. PHIVOLCS reported no significant seismic events at the time.

reconstructed_article: American botanist Lou Jost has discovered the world's smallest orchid among the roots of a larger plant in a nature reserve in Ecuador. The flowers measure 2.1mm wide and have transparent petals that are only one cell thick. The finding surpasses the previous record held by Platystele jungermannioides, which has 2.5mm flowers. Jost discovered the new species accidentally while examining a larger plant collected from the reserve in eastern Ecuador. The reserve was created by a British organization in partnership with Fundacion EcoMinga, for which Jost works. Ecuador has been the site of discovery of more than 1,000 new orchid species in the past century. Jost stated that he found the tiny plant among the roots of another small orchid he had collected and taken to his greenhouse to flower. Months later, he noticed the smaller plant among the roots and recognized it as more significant than the larger orchid. He noted that examining the flower is often the best method for identifying orchid species and determining whether a specimen is unknown. The newly discovered orchid belongs to the same genus as the previous record holder. It is the 60th new orchid species that Dr. Jost has discovered in the past decade.

reconstructed_article: On Friday, airborne asbestos was discovered at Renaissance Middle School in Montclair, New Jersey, leading to the evacuation of more than 200 students and the school's closure. The school, part of Montclair Public Schools, remained closed Monday and Tuesday for asbestos testing and cleaning. A letter from the Superintendent's Office said plaster may have been disturbed during Thursday construction on new fire doors. An inspection arranged by the school district found asbestos in the plaster, and a subsequent inspection by asbestos consultant Detail Associates detected airborne asbestos fiber levels above the acceptable range in the third floor hallway. Business administrator Dana Sullivan said testing on March 31 confirmed asbestos in a brown undercoating of plaster. The affected area was sealed off. Public Information Officer Laura Federico said sixth and seventh graders were transported to Hillside Elementary School and eighth graders to another location. Detail Associates conducted cleaning on Saturday. At a Monday meeting with parents, district officials were asked to include lockers in the cleanup, prompting Tuesday's closure. Steve Jaraczewski of Detail Associates said one of four test samples was positive for airborne asbestos at more than six times acceptable levels. He criticized the asbestos management plan provided by the Archdiocese of Newark, which owns the building. Archdiocese representative Jim Goodness said the building would reopen soon. The state Department of Environmental Protection is supervising the cleanup.

reconstructed_article: The Christchurch Mail Centre in New Zealand was evacuated Friday after employees refused to continue working due to exposure to heavy amounts of dust suspected to be asbestos. Tuam 2 Ltd, the company set to convert the 27-year-old Christchurch Mail Centre into a new city council building, has been aware of the presence of asbestos in the building since May 2008. Hawkins Construction contacted authorities voicing concerns of possible exposure to asbestos material. Testing is currently underway at the facility to determine the nature of the exposure. The Christchurch Mail Centre is operated by New Zealand Post. According to Christchurch Delivery Business Leader Duncan Burman, approximately 50 post workers operate out of the facility, which services about 35,000 addresses in the central Christchurch region. Tony Marryatt, chief executive of the city council, was asked by Councillor Helen Broughton for an explanation of the incident. Broughton, the only councillor who voted against construction of new city council buildings, said she wanted to see the professional opinion from a building consultant who had assessed the building. The owners of the Christchurch Mail Centre informed New Zealand Post that testing performed in November confirmed there was no asbestos in the area. Anna Kenny, a spokesperson for the New Zealand trade union, said concerns were raised about plumes of dust Friday morning suspected to be asbestos, but there has been no confirmation. Kenny confirmed that no asbestos was found in a check of the building in November, but requested further air quality checks before workers return.

reconstructed_article: Tropical Storm Danielle has strengthened into a hurricane with winds up to 130 km/h (80 mph) and is headed towards Bermuda. Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center in Miami, Florida expect it to strengthen further over the next two days. Hurricane Danielle is the second hurricane of the 2010 Atlantic hurricane season. The storm formed near the Cape Verde Islands off the coast of West Africa, initially classified as Tropical Depression Six, before developing into a more organized cyclone. Meteorologists predict Danielle will be the first of several storms to form within the next two weeks, as the Atlantic hurricane season reaches its peak. Rick Knabb of the National Hurricane Center stated, "There are signs that the Atlantic is acting like it should in August and September. We're seeing more activity than we did earlier in the season." Meanwhile, North America is simultaneously threatened by Tropical Storm Frank, an 80 km/h (50 mph) storm in the Pacific Ocean located about 210 km (130 miles) south-southwest of Acapulco, Mexico. Mexico has issued a tropical storm watch for the area. Although the 2010 season appears to be one with low activity, emergency officials continue to stress safety and awareness to residents in hurricane-prone areas. Lauren McKeague of the Florida Division of Emergency Management said, "It only takes one storm to cause a loss of lives and devastating property damage." Hurricane Andrew was cited as a catastrophic Category 5 storm that occurred during a lower-than-average season.

reconstructed_article: Ministers from 13 Asian countries pledged on Friday to double the wild tiger population on the continent to 7,000 by 2022. The commitment was made in Thailand at Asia's first ministerial conference on tiger conservation. The 13 countries endorsing the pledge were Bangladesh, Bhutan, Cambodia, China, India, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, Nepal, Russia, Thailand, and Vietnam, all countries where the wild Asian tiger is still found. Thai Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva said in a video address that the wild tiger is in crisis and that this may be the last chance to save it. The meeting was partly organized by the Global Tiger Initiative, a coalition within the World Bank, as well as the Smithsonian Institution and various conservation groups. Meeting host Suwit Khunkitti, Thailand's minister of natural resources and environment, noted that there were 100,000 tigers across range countries 100 years ago, compared with about 3,500 today. According to the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), tiger numbers have declined due to poaching. The animals live in only seven percent of the territory they occupied a century ago, according to Voice of America. WWF representative Michael Baltzer said it was important to act during the Year of the Tiger. Global Tiger Initiative program director Keshav Varma said saving the tiger also preserves habitat for other species and draws attention to issues including encroachment and corruption.

reconstructed_article: Maricopa County, Arizona, Sheriff Joe Arpaio is expected to endorse Republican presidential candidate Rick Perry of Texas at a New Hampshire campaign event, according to sources. Arpaio is expected to appear with Perry today and will remain in the state for three days. Arpaio, who calls himself "America's Toughest Sheriff," is known for his stance on illegal immigration. As Sheriff, he has led raids to arrest illegal immigrants and supported Arizona's stringent immigration law. GOP presidential candidates Michele Bachmann, Herman Cain, and Mitt Romney sought his endorsement. He endorsed Romney in 2008. The endorsement could help Perry with voters who have had concerns about his record on illegal immigration. Perry was criticized for signing a bill granting in-state tuition benefits to college-age illegal immigrants. He defended the bill during a September presidential debate, saying those criticizing him "don't have a heart." He later backed down from the statement. As Governor of Texas for eleven years, Perry has overseen the state with the longest border with Mexico. He vetoed a bill that would have allowed illegal immigrants to receive driver's licenses and signed another requiring identification to vote. During his presidential campaign, Perry opposed the proposed full-length border fence, calling it impractical. He favors targeted fencing combined with mobilization of enforcement personnel.

reconstructed_article: More than 1,700 women from over 40 countries marched in Goma, Democratic Republic of the Congo, to protest sexual violence against women. The United Nations has called the country the "rape capital of the world" and estimates 15,000 rapes occurred in the DRC last year. A local activist said the women have had enough of the civil war, the rape, and the lack of attention to their situation. Both rebel groups and government troops are accused of rape. Organizers said the march aimed to draw international attention to the issue. Eastern Congo is the most affected region, and aid groups have suggested the actual number of rapes may be higher because victims are unlikely to come forward. The UN says mass rapes have occurred in the area for at least 15 years. Some rape victims left the hospital to participate in the march. The third "World March of Women" followed several days of talks aimed at changing the social acceptance of violence, especially against women, in the Congo. Peace and development were also on the agenda for women from nations including Togo, South Africa, Pakistan, and Brazil. Some men also joined the discussions.

reconstructed_article: Senator Campbell praised supermarket shoppers and operators for cutting three billion plastic bags from circulation over the past two years. A report compiled by a body representing major supermarkets showed that by the end of last year, supermarkets had reduced their annual use of lightweight, single-use bags by 45 per cent compared with 2002. Senator Campbell said the cutback means fewer bags in the litter stream and that the goal is to stop plastic bags entering the litter stream and spoiling Australia's environment. He said the result came from voluntary action, with no regulations, levies, or additional costs to shoppers. Major supermarkets are committed to achieving a 50 per cent reduction goal by the end of this year. Campbell also said development of a viable degradable bag to replace existing lightweight plastic ones is key to further reductions. Environmentalists say plastic bags have had a severe impact on Australia's natural environment. Plastic bags can take between 20 and 1000 years to break down. An estimated 6.67 billion or 36,700 tonnes of plastic bags are disposed of in landfill sites throughout Australia each year. Many thousands of marine mammals and seabirds die every year worldwide as a result of plastic litter. A 2004 NSW Parliamentary paper reported that plastic bags are of significant concern in the marine and aquatic environment, as aquatic life can be threatened through entanglement, suffocation, and ingestion.

reconstructed_article: Democrats.com, a progressive organization, is offering a $1,000 reward to anyone who can get U.S. President George W. Bush to answer a question about pre-war intelligence. The contest follows Bush's month-long refusal to answer questions about a leaked secret memo stating that "the intelligence and facts were being fixed around the policy." Neither the U.S. nor UK government has disputed the document's accuracy. The question asks whether Bush and his administration "fixed" intelligence about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and terrorism ties to justify the invasion of Iraq. An additional $100 is offered to anyone who asks Bush the question, with video evidence required. The reward money came from small donations to the website. The contest occurs amid renewed criticism from citizens, members of Congress, retired politicians, and constitutional lawyers following the leak of British documents. Earlier in the month, White House spokesman Scott McClellan told reporters the administration saw "no need" to respond to a congressional letter about the memo, stating that public comments before the war showed how intelligence was used. One pre-war justification was that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction, none of which were found. The Senate Intelligence Committee is considering three possibilities: the weapons were moved, CIA intelligence was flawed, or satisfactory intelligence was mishandled by the administration. The last possibility has not been formally investigated.

He acknowledged Denmark is in a similar position to the UK, with the Danish government working closely with the United States and the United Kingdom over Iraq and Afghanistan.

Security in Denmark has been increased at airports, rail stations, ports, borders, and other public places.

The Australian Government is building a detention facility on Christmas Island, 1,400 km off Australia's northwest coast, at a cost of $210 million and with capacity for 800 beds. Construction began in January 2005, and the facility is scheduled to be operational by late 2006. A DIMIA spokesperson said the facility would serve as an immigration reception and processing centre, and that a review of mainland detention centres would likely follow its completion.

Christmas Island Shire President Gordon Thompson said residents were concerned about impacts on tourism, restricted access to fishing and snorkelling areas, and lack of consultation. He said the Shire council was not notified when the existing Christmas Island detention centre reopened on November 17 to detain seven West Timorese asylum seekers. Azmi Yon, president of the island's Malay association, said locals sought written clarification on the facility's purpose.

Democrats senator Andrew Bartlett said transferring asylum seekers to the remote location denied them proper processing and legal access. Greens senator Kerry Nettle called for construction to be suspended, citing existing detention capacity of 3,975 people across facilities including Baxter, Villawood, Maribyrnong, Perth, Port Augusta, Port Hedland, and Woomera.

Environmental concerns were raised because the site is adjacent to Abbott's Booby habitat within Christmas Island National Park. Research indicated nesting birds within 300 metres of clearings experienced lower breeding success, with 36% of breeding sites in that zone. The Wilderness Society criticised the government's self-exemption from EPBC Act environmental scrutiny.

reconstructed_article: Following the ousting of Thailand's Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra, anti-coup protesters in Bangkok began using a three-finger salute—curling the little finger and thumb into the palm and raising the three middle fingers—last weekend. The gesture originates from The Hunger Games book and film series. Thailand's military junta, the National Council for Peace and Order, announced on Tuesday its intent to arrest protesters displaying the gesture. Colonel Weerachon Sukhondhapatipak told the Associated Press that authorities are monitoring the movement and will control obvious forms of resistance to prevent disorder. Colonel Winthai Suwaree expressed a similar sentiment to media. The coup, reportedly Thailand's fourteenth since the adoption of constitutional monarchy in 1932, followed political deadlock from demonstrations spanning seven months. A midnight-to-4 a.m. curfew remains in effect, with Phuket and other beach resorts exempted to protect the tourist industry. The United States Department of State advised citizens to reconsider non-essential travel to Thailand and avoid protest groups. The junta imposed internet censorship, television broadcast restrictions, and banned political assemblies of five or more people. On Sunday, approximately 6,000 soldiers and police officers were deployed in Bangkok to suppress protests, with protesters also using flash mobs and masked walks through the central shopping district. Some protesters interpreted the gesture as representing freedom, election, and democracy. Social activist Sombat Boonngam-anong, belonging to a protest group supporting the Shinawatra governments, advocated silent protest raising three fingers three times daily for 30 seconds at 9 a.m., 1 p.m., and 5 p.m.

The document, released by state news agency Xinhua, says that while "notable" progress has been made in fighting corruption, efforts need to be more effective. It warns of corruption within government and cites new regulations requiring officials to report investment and income. The report also credits the Internet and media for exposing corruption.

China has launched several anti-corruption campaigns in recent years. A Chinese anti-corruption researcher told Xinhua the report indicated the government now has "a more open and cooperative attitude toward the problem."

Several high-profile corruption cases have occurred. This year, Wen Qiang, the highest-ranking justice official in Chongqing, was executed for accepting bribes, shielding criminal gangs, and rape. In 2008, a powerful party boss was jailed for 18 years for involvement in a corruption scandal.

The report says that despite efforts to combat corruption, eliminating it completely will be difficult. It notes that because relevant mechanisms and systems remain incomplete, corruption persists, with some cases involving huge sums of money. The situation in combating corruption remains very serious, and the tasks are still abundant.

reconstructed_article: Corus, the world's fifth largest steel producer, announced on Friday that it may be forced to mothball its steelworks in Teesside, England, threatening the jobs of 1,920 employees. Corus' chief executive, Kirby Adams, said he was extremely disappointed that the consortium members had taken this action. Business Secretary Peter Mandelson said it is essential that Corus does everything it can legally, and with the government's assistance, to reinstate the agreement. British Prime Minister Gordon Brown said the government was doing everything in its power to ensure that the contract is upheld. Mandelson also said the government was not prepared to reconcile itself to the inevitable closure of the plant. The leader of Redcar and Cleveland Council, Councillor George Dunning, described the announcement as being hit by a mini earthquake. Liberal Democrats including Simon Hughes, Fiona Hall, and Stephen Hughes MEP supported the idea that the government should subsidise wages at the plant on a temporary basis. Hughes and Hall suggested the government should apply to the EU's European Globalisation Fund. Adams said the move could bring to an end a heritage of steelmaking at Teesside. Corus said a 90-day consultation period is due to begin. Corus' owner, Tata Steel, is also facing difficulties with another UK operation, automobile company Jaguar Land Rover.

reconstructed_article: Bach Technology announced MusicDNA at the end of January, a new music file format intended to replace MP3. MusicDNA uses compression methods similar to MP3 but adds an XML file defining additional content, including lyrics, artwork, tour dates, blog posts, videos, and Twitter feeds. The files also contain audio analysis information intended to improve search, recommendation, and playlist tools. Bach Technology CEO Stefan Kohlmeyer stated that MusicDNA has been in development since the company's founding in 2007. Bach holds a strategic partnership with Fraunhofer IDMT, whose CEO Karlheinz Brandenburg, credited with inventing the MP3, participates in research and development discussions. Unlike iTunes LP, MusicDNA is built on open standards and is platform-agnostic, allowing transfer between devices and purchase of individual tracks rather than complete albums. Additional content updates dynamically when the user is online. Only paid files receive dynamic updates, which Bach Technology describes as an incentive to purchase legitimate files rather than using peer-to-peer networks. Mark Mulligan, vice president and research director at Forrester Research, told a UK newspaper that innovations like iTunes LP need to go further, suggesting people should pay once for regularly updated content. Kohlmeyer noted that MP3 was developed over twenty years ago and does not add to the listening experience beyond portability. MusicDNA rollout is staggered over 2010, with beta versions around Easter and full commercial rollout expected in summer.

reconstructed_article: U.S. officials announced new plans requiring air traffic controllers to have longer rest periods between shifts after a series of incidents in which controllers fell asleep on duty at airports across the country. The union representing controllers in the U.S. said it had full support for the new steps.

reconstructed_article: Roger D. Kornberg of the United States won the 2006 Nobel Prize for chemistry for his studies of the molecular basis of eukaryotic transcription. His work explains how information encoded in DNA is used to produce the proteins that keep cells functioning. Eukaryotes are multi-celled organisms, such as animals, plants and fungi, which have their genetic material stored in nuclei within their cells. To use their genetic information, eukaryotes extract bits of the coded information via the formation of messenger RNA, which consists of copies of a particular gene within the DNA strand. Translation takes place when proteins are built from the information transcribed with the messenger RNA. Eukaryotic transcription is vital for life. If transcription is interrupted, as can happen when cells are exposed to certain toxins, the cells will die. Kornberg documented eukaryotic transcription with snapshots of the process in action. He created the snapshots by crystallizing cellular material partway through transcription and exposing them to x-rays that produced patterns revealing the intermediate structures. Kornberg's work may lead to novel drugs and medical treatments. Kornberg's father Arthur Kornberg won the Nobel Prize in physiology and medicine in 1959 for explaining how organisms synthesize DNA from nucleotides.

reconstructed_article: JJB Sports, a British sports clothing and equipment retail chain, is making 2,200 employees in the United Kingdom redundant as it enters administration. In a £24m deal, Sports Direct has agreed to purchase and rebrand 20 stores, as well as purchase the brand, stock, website, the license to the Slazenger Golf brand, and JJB's Wigan headquarters. The deal with Sports Direct will keep 500 employees in work. Additionally, 167 employees will continue working for JJB while KPMG, the appointed administrators, winds the company down. The bulk of the money from the Sports Direct deal will go toward repaying loans made by Bank of Scotland, as well as money owed to the sports clothing brand Adidas and the American sports retailer Dick's Sporting Goods, which had previously invested £20m in JJB. Shareholders are not expected to receive any payout. Former professional footballer and JJB owner Dave Whelan, who founded the company in 1971 and sold his share in 2007, decided not to invest to save the business. He told the BBC that when he sold it, approximately five years prior, it was valued at a billion pounds, and now it is completely worthless.

reconstructed_article: After Atlanta, Georgia, lost its bid to host Wikimania 2008, which was awarded to Alexandria, Egypt, organizers began planning a Conference of the Americas focused on Wikimedia in the Americas. The conference is scheduled for May 15-18, 2008, at the Georgia Institute of Technology in Atlanta. One organizer, an unpaid intern at the Wikimedia Foundation offices in St. Petersburg, Florida, said planning discussions began before the Wikimania location was announced and that the conference was not created in retaliation or to compete with Wikimania. He said the goal is to provide a Wikimedia event for the western hemisphere, noting that travel to Egypt is more expensive for people in the region. Over 100 interested parties across the United States have expressed interest in volunteering or attending. The conference will cover Wikimedia and the free culture movement in relation to communities in North America, including the United States and Canada, and Latin America. A journalism segment will be held at the Turner Broadcasting building on Techwood Drive in Midtown Atlanta. Wikimedia Argentina and the Wikimedia Foundation have received proposals for endorsement, with decisions pending. Sponsors include Georgia Tech, the Public Journalism Network, and the Carolina Open Source Initiative. The selection of Alexandria for Wikimania 2008 prompted discussion on public mailing lists regarding safety, free speech, and the jury's decision process.

reconstructed_article: NASA reported that a three-inch gouge was found in the heat shield on one of Endeavour's wings. The gouge was observed as the shuttle approached the International Space Station (ISS) and was captured on camera by ISS astronauts. According to NASA, the gouge was located on a six-inch thick tile on the starboard wing of the heat shield and may have been caused by ice rather than foam. NASA expressed concern because the hole appears to be deep. Mission management team chairman John Shannon stated that the assessment would involve thermal analysis based on the damage, a review of flight history, and testing of the area. He noted that it was too early to determine whether repairs were required. If the damage is irreversible and cannot be fixed, the Endeavour crew would remain on the ISS. NASA stated that supplies would last until a rescue mission could be launched on October 8. During Endeavour's liftoff on August 8, cameras showed moisture on the lens, but the object causing the damage was not captured. At least nine pieces of debris were filmed during takeoff, though NASA said only three had a possibility of hitting the shuttle. Astronauts were expected to use a laser attached to the shuttle's robotic arm to measure the gouge's depth and size on Sunday. Potential repairs included affixing a metal plate over the tile, filling it with putty, or sealing the gouge.

reconstructed_article: The British Association of Dermatologists (BAD) released a report identifying an illness termed 'mobile phone dermatitis,' in which cell phone users develop a rash on the side of their face. BAD attributed the condition to nickel deposits in the metal components of some phones. Nickel is known to cause rashes in individuals with sensitivity or allergy to the metal. BAD stated that the condition is likely to affect people who spend extended time talking on the phone, with prolonged text messaging or calling most likely to produce rashes on the face, ears, or fingertips. Tests conducted in January on 22 cellular phones by scientists in Rhode Island, United States, found that 10 contained nickel, while the remainder had rubber buttons and plastic cases. Researcher Lionel Bercovitch, MD, stated in the journal of the Canadian Medical Association on January 1, 2008, that phones designed for rugged use often have rubber coating and no surface nickel, while those with fashionable designs often have metallic accents and are more likely to contain free nickel. Researchers noted that prolonged or continuous exposure to nickel can cause severe reactions even in individuals not previously allergic. BAD dermatologist Dr. Graham Lowe said prolonged or repetitive contact with a nickel-containing phone is more likely to cause a skin reaction in those who are allergic. BAD stated that in the United Kingdom alone, nearly 30% of the population suffers from rashes caused by prolonged exposure to nickel. Researchers recommended that individuals purchase swab test kits to test for traces of nickel.

reconstructed_article: George Smoot of the United States and John Mather of NASA shared the 2006 Nobel Prize in Physics for their discovery of the blackbody form and anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background radiation. The Nobel Prize Committee cited the physicists for their work on the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) project. COBE revealed fluctuations in faint microwave signals from space that are thought to be remnants of the Big Bang. Although the precise origin of the fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background is not yet clear, they may represent clumps in the very early universe that led to the galaxies seen today. Prior to the COBE map of the universe, it was unclear why the universe contained stars and galaxies rather than an evenly distributed dust cloud. Theorists had predicted that a sensitive measurement of microwaves from the sky would reveal minute temperature fluctuations, which represent variations in the density of matter in the early universe. The denser portions served as seeds for galaxies that formed later. COBE was the first experiment sensitive enough to confirm the predicted temperature variations encoded in the map of the microwave background. The initial discovery of the Cosmic Microwave Background by Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson led to their award of the 1978 Nobel Prize in physics. Although they measured the approximate temperature of the universe to be about 3.5 kelvins, their ground-based microwave telescope could not pick out the detail available to COBE.

reconstructed_article: On February 2, 2008, approximately 100 people gathered in Orlando, Florida, to protest against the Church of Scientology. The protest was organized by the Internet-based group Anonymous as part of its Project Chanology movement. Anonymous formed the movement in response to what it views as suppression of information on the Internet by the Church of Scientology. The group was initially motivated by the Church of Scientology's attempts to remove a promotional video featuring Scientologist Tom Cruise from the Internet. The Church of Scientology issued legal complaints to YouTube and Gawker; YouTube removed the video, but Gawker refused to do so. Project Chanology participants took down several Scientology websites in mid-January using denial-of-service attacks. The group organized a series of protests outside Church of Scientology centers worldwide on February 10, 2008, with at least 217 protests expected across cities including New York City, Montreal, Houston, London, Melbourne, and Los Angeles. Protestors in Orlando held signs with messages including "Knowledge is Free Scientology Isn't," "Who Is Xenu?", "www.xenu.net," and "Honk if you hate Scientology." An unnamed organizer told the Orlando Sentinel that the group was protesting "a gross violation of the right to see free church material," referring to the Tom Cruise video. Protestors claimed the Church of Scientology is a "dangerous cult" and said the organization is responsible for crimes and deaths.

reconstructed_article: The 108-floor central component of the new World Trade Center in New York City has been officially renamed 1 World Trade Center, ending the Freedom Tower name it had carried since 2003. The building is on track for completion in 2013, with 10 floors partially finished. Port Authority of New York and New Jersey Chairman Anthony Coscia said the name is easiest for people to identify with and has received a warm reception. Former Governor George Pataki, who revealed the Freedom Tower name nearly six years ago, criticized the switch, stating the building is not simply real estate or a marketing name. 1 World Trade Center has been the building's legal name and address for two years, with the public change prompted by increased construction and lease marketing. reconstructed_article: The University of Southern California developed a simulation system called Virtual Iraq to provide realistic battlefield effects. The fully-immersive system was created as part of a therapy to help soldiers with post-traumatic stress disorder manage their psychological issues. Professor Paul Sharkey, Director of the Visualization Center at the University of Reading, developed the system with two professors from the USC Institute for Creative Technologies, Albert Rizzo and Jarrell Pair. They created a virtual room at the Visualization Center where patients can experience battlefield effects. The system provides sounds, sights, and smells of the battlefield so soldiers and military staff experience combat scenarios in a low-threat context. Therapists can add elements to the virtual world, including the smell of burning rubber, the sound of gunfire, and the buzzing of a helicopter. To date, four patients have been treated, and all reported improvement in their symptoms. Scientists state that the aim of the system is to re-expose patients to relevant traumatic events without re-traumatizing them. They seek to manage patients' emotional responses to make them more flexible in everyday situations.

reconstructed_article: International twin-study researchers conducted parallel genetic studies into bipolar disorder and schizophrenia, examining more than 50,000 people worldwide. Eleven genetic regions were identified; seven were for schizophrenia, five of which were previously undiscovered. Two genetic loci were associated with both diseases. The studies scanned genomes of both healthy and afflicted individuals. Researchers found that genetic factors are numerous rather than a single faulty gene. In schizophrenia, at most around 30% of genetic components are thought to have been identified. Pablo Gejman, a lead researcher on the schizophrenia study, stated that one goal of genetic research is to find druggable targets. He identified calcium-activated channels in the brain as candidates for new drugs, linked to schizophrenia in the study. A genetic locus called mir137 suggests an abnormality of gene regulation. The team found no evidence that dopamine receptors are involved, though current drug treatments target them. Professor Rodney Scott from the University of Newcastle in Australia said the strength of the research lies in its numbers, providing robust statistical power. Both Gejman and Scott described the study as highly reliable due to its sample size. Scott noted that the two shared genetic loci are suggestive of a potential common pathway giving rise to both diseases. Gejman called it an excellent demonstration because the same chains are common to both disorders. Each illness affects approximately 1% of people. The diseases are poorly understood, and it remains uncertain whether they are components of a single spectrum or comprise multiple illnesses.

reconstructed_article: U.S. District Judge Stein ruled that the use of a 25-second clip from John Lennon's song "Imagine" in a film critical of religion is likely defensible under the fair use doctrine. The film "Expelled," produced by Premise Media and starring comedian Ben Stein, uses the clip to represent what Premise representative Anthony Falzone described at a hearing as "the most popular and persuasive embodiment of this viewpoint that the world is better off without religion." In the song, Lennon proposes the hypothetical "Imagine there's no heaven ... and no religion too." On April 23, 2008, Lennon's widow, Yoko Ono, along with his sons Sean and Julian, and music producer EMI Blackwood, Inc., filed suit against Premise Media seeking damages for alleged copyright infringement, as the song had not been licensed for use in the film. On May 19, a preliminary injunction was issued preventing distribution of the film. On June 2, Judge Stein ruled that the fair use defense would likely succeed and lifted the injunction, writing that "the fair use of a copyrighted work for the purposes of criticism and commentary is not an infringement of copyright." "Expelled" is a documentary claiming that intelligent design proponents are being suppressed by the scientific community. It has received criticism from scientists and film critics and has faced copyright claims over animated sequences resembling "The Inner Life of the Cell," produced by XVIVO and Harvard University. Ono stated that "it is a pity that this decision weakens the rights of all copyright owners" and plans to appeal.

On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted 269-152 to reject the Net Neutrality Amendment to the COPE Act. The COPE Act, which aims to make it easier for telecommunications companies to offer cable TV service and strengthen competition, passed by a 321-101 vote the same day. Proponents said it would lower high-speed Internet prices by enabling providers to bundle phone, data, video, and mobile services. It was the first major telecommunications bill before Congress in over a decade.

The Net Neutrality amendment sought to require broadband providers to treat all data equally, specifying a duty not to block, impair, degrade, discriminate against, or interfere with access to lawful content, applications, or services. Its passage would have prevented companies such as AT&T, Verizon, and Comcast from charging content providers like Google, Yahoo, Amazon, or eBay for priority network access.

Democrats largely supported the amendment, with 140 voting in favor and 58 against, while 11 Republicans voted for it and 211 against. House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi argued that additional fees would burden small web-based businesses and hamper noncommercial communications. Phone companies and Congressional allies argued the restrictions would discourage investment in network upgrades. The bill is due to be discussed next in the Senate.

Liam Aitchison's family criticized comments made on the British television programme The Wright Stuff about his murder. During Tuesday's broadcast, host Matthew Wright said "there's been another murder" in a false Scottish accent, referencing the UK crime drama Taggart. Panelist Charlie Baker remarked the investigation would be like "the longest episode of Taggart of all time," and the audience laughed.

Liam Aitchison's family issued a statement calling the comments "insensitive and offensive" and "very upsetting and insulting for, not just the family, but for the whole community of the Western Isles." His father, Norman Aitchison, wrote on the programme's website that he was "disgusted" and asked whether panel members would joke if it were their own child.

On the following day's broadcast, Wright said he would "like to apologise" if viewers were offended, stating there was no intention to belittle the tragedy. Channel 5's spokeswoman said Wright's apology was "clear." Wright noted he had not been helped by campaigns urging people to report him to Ofcom, a UK media regulator, and advised such people to "grow up." Channel 5 removed Tuesday's episode from its website.

Angus MacNeil, MP for Na h-Eileanan an Iar, described Wright's behaviour as "beyond belief" and intended to complain to Ofcom. Comhairle nan Eilean Siar also complained. A Facebook page titled "Report The Wright Stuff to Ofcom" attracted over two thousand likes. Ofcom was assessing complaints but had not decided whether to investigate.

McClain County District Attorney Tim Kuykendall said the body was in a storage bin in the bedroom closet. Underwood was arrested on suspicion of first-degree murder and held without bail. He had no prior criminal record or history of mental illness. Bolin was last seen Wednesday near the Purcell public library, and her family reported her missing that night. Officials issued an Amber Alert on Thursday night, noting no abduction had been reported initially. Underwood drew suspicion at an information checkpoint set up at the apartment complex. Police found a decorative dagger, hacksaw, barbecue skewers, meat tenderizer, and wooden cutting board in his apartment. Preliminary autopsy reports indicated Bolin died of asphyxiation and blunt force trauma to the head. Authorities said deep saw marks on the body indicated an attempt to decapitate her. Police suspected postmortem molestation, as the body was found unclothed. Purcell police chief David Tompkins stated the motive appeared to involve a plan to kidnap, rape, torture, kill, decapitate, drain of blood, rape the corpse, eat the corpse, and dispose of the organs and bones. Kuykendall said Underwood reported fantasizing about eating someone beginning a year prior. Authorities believed other individuals, including a woman and a 5-year-old boy, had been targeted and considered. Kuykendall stated he intended to seek the death penalty.

reconstructed_article: At least ten attackers armed with knives and dressed in black attacked a train station in Kunming, China, yesterday. At least 28 victims were killed and 113 wounded, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua. The local municipal government accused separatist forces for the attack. Xinhua described the incident as an organized, premeditated violent terrorist attack. One suspect was arrested, while four or five suspects were shot dead. Yang Haifei, a local resident, told Xinhua that the attackers rushed in and began attacking people while he was buying a ticket. He stated that a person came at him with a long knife and he fled with others, while people who were slower were attacked and fell on the ground. Preparations are underway for an annual legislature meeting, at which President Xi Jinping and his government are to deliver their first one-year work report on Wednesday. Xi Jinping stated there should be all-out efforts to apprehend the attackers. The Security Management Bureau stated law enforcement will crack down on the crimes in accordance with the law without tolerance. He called for severe punishments in accordance with the law and to crack down on those responsible. China has also blamed a suicide attack in Beijing late last year on separatists.
